current_answer: As of 9 September 2026 at 06:10 UTC, the strongest new evidence is a route, access, and safety-behavior problem, not a broad model collapse. OpenAI documents plan-, surface-, model-, and effort-dependent usage; Anthropic documents safety-triggered fallback from Fable 5.1; and a Google AI Studio developer thread reports Pro-to-Flash-Lite routing on long prompts, though Google has not confirmed it. OpenAI, Claude, and Grok status pages were operational at the check; a scoped Codex tracker is nominal and Claude Code’s public detector is still collecting a baseline. User pain can still be real in a route, safety, context, tool, or budget layer. Confidence: high for declared and provider-documented behavior; medium for the narrow Gemini route lead; low for a general capability decline.
summary: The newest lead is a serving-route problem: a Google developer report says long Pro requests may finish on Flash Lite, but the report is not provider-confirmed.

Provider documentation makes safety fallback and budget part of the served system: Anthropic describes Fable fallback behavior, and OpenAI describes plan-, model-, effort-, and task-dependent allowance.
OpenAI, Claude, and Grok status pages were operational at the check; recent declared incidents are recovery evidence, not a model-quality score.
A direct Codex/SWE-Bench-Pro tracker remains nominal, while the public Claude Code detector is explicitly collecting a new baseline; neither covers every consumer surface.
Field reports still describe refusals, context loss, correction cost, gibberish, and quota pressure, with positive counterreports showing that quality and cost can move in opposite directions.
Best next move: record the visible and final served model, surface, plan, effort, context, task cost, and status; then replay a matched task before switching.
uncertainty: Declared provider records describe stated incidents and designed behavior, not every account or route.
The Gemini route report is technically detailed but unconfirmed and small.
Community pain is task-level and mixed; no public same-task consumer baseline covers the major surfaces.
Cross-sectional benchmarks and rolling field metrics cannot alone prove a longitudinal regression.
Analytics for this pool were unavailable, so no first-party prevalence or retention signal was used.
